title: The Jewish people
hook: John Paul II visited Rome's synagogue in 1986 and spoke of elder brothers

segments.voice: Yesterday, other Christians: Methodists, Baptists, Pentecostals, joined by one baptism. Your line was brothers and sisters in Christ. Did you nod to a church that isn't yours? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

The synagogue of Rome stands by the Tiber, a short way from the Vatican. In 1986, Pope John Paul the Second crossed that short distance and went in, as a guest. Rome's chief rabbi, Elio Toaff, welcomed him. The two men stood side by side before the congregation. And the pope spoke to the Jewish people in front of him as his brothers, his dearly loved brothers, and, in a certain way, his elder brothers. Today, the Jewish people.
screen: `A SYNAGOGUE BY THE TIBER.` → `A POPE CROSSES A SHORT DISTANCE.` → `IN A CERTAIN WAY, ELDER BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: First, where the pope's words came from. At the Second Vatican Council, the declaration Nostra Aetate spoke of a spiritual bond linking the Church with the stock of Abraham. It said the Church received the revelation of the Old Testament through the people with whom God made the ancient covenant. It also deplored hatred, persecutions and displays of antisemitism directed against Jews at any time and by anyone. Second, a verse the council leaned on. Paul, writing to the Romans about his own people, says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance." The council drew from this that God does not take back his gifts or his call. Later Catholic teaching put it plainly: the old covenant has never been revoked. Third, why elder. In a family, the elder sibling was there first. The pope's word carried both closeness and humility: Christians come after, and owe a debt. He also recalled the long history of suffering, and repeated the council's words deploring hatred and persecution. Jews understand their covenant and their life on their own terms, not as part of a Christian story. Some Jewish readers have welcomed the phrase; others have noted that in Genesis, elder brothers don't always fare well. Both reactions are part of the conversation. Last, look back at this week. The Holy See. Canon law, for souls. Spiritual ecumenism, prayer first. Anglicans, old friends. Lutherans, from conflict to communion. Other Christians, brothers and sisters. Today the circle reaches past the churches entirely, to the people whose olive tree, in Paul's image, Christians were grafted onto.
screen: `A SPIRITUAL BOND WITH ABRAHAM'S STOCK.` · `THE GIFTS AND THE CALLING OF GOD.` · `ELDER: CLOSENESS AND HUMILITY.` · `A WEEK OF NEIGHBORS, AND THE ROOT.` · then, large: `WITHOUT REPENTANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Jewish neighbors. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a synagogue in your town, or a Jewish friend, coworker or neighbor. Think of their week: a Sabbath meal, a school run, a prayer said in Hebrew, a worry you may know nothing about. Hold them for a few breaths. If you pray, you can pray for their peace and safety, in your own simple words or in silence. If you don't pray, hold them in mind with respect and goodwill. The bell holds the time.
The Jewish people. In Catholic teaching, the people of the covenant God has not revoked, whom a pope called, in a certain way, elder brothers. Today's word.
Your line: elder brothers. Today, if you read or hear any verse from the Psalms or the prophets, remember whose prayers they were first. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church holds an ongoing dialogue with the Jewish people through a Vatican commission for religious relations with the Jews, and popes have visited synagogues. Locally, parishes and synagogues sometimes hold joint study, service and remembrance.

fork.setup: you're John Paul II, standing in the synagogue of Rome beside its chief rabbi. how do you address the people before you?
options: as strangers you hope to convert.
as your brothers, in a certain way your elder brothers.
fork.reveal: he spoke of them as dearly loved brothers and, in a certain way, elder brothers, words rooted in the council's teaching on the bond with Abraham's stock.

trapdoor: what you thought: elder brothers is just a polite phrase.
what it means: it says Jews were there first, and that the Church owes a debt to the people of the ancient covenant.
what a scholar hears: Nostra Aetate 4 leans on Romans 11:29, that the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.

sources.ref: John Paul II, Address at the Synagogue of Rome, 13 April 1986

notes: Editor pass: 'covenant not revoked' now attributed to later Catholic teaching (CCC 121 added to sources), since Nostra Aetate does not say it in those words; the address line now says the pope repeated the council's deploring of persecution rather than an unsourced 'Church's sorrow'; 'of course' cut; 'the people Paul called the root' (Paul's root is ambiguous) changed to his grafted olive-tree image.
Week end: the teach looks back at days 1415–1420 (Holy See, canon law, spiritual ecumenism, Anglicans, Lutherans, other Christians).
The year 1986 is stated in the voice because it is in the index hook and the cited address is dated 13 April 1986; confirm under the claims rule. Elio Toaff as chief rabbi: confirm.

The address is paraphrased ('our dearly beloved brothers and, in a certain way, our elder brothers'); the Vatican translation is not public domain. 'He also spoke there of the long history of suffering, and of the Church's sorrow': confirm against the address, which recalled the Shoah and deplored persecution.

Nostra Aetate 4 paraphrased: spiritual bond linking the people of the New Covenant with Abraham's stock; the Church received the revelation of the Old Testament through that people; God does not repent of the gifts he makes (citing Romans 11:28–29); decries hatred, persecutions, displays of anti-Semitism. 'The covenant ... has not been revoked' reflects later teaching (John Paul II at Mainz, CCC 121); confirm framing.
Jewish reactions to 'elder brothers' are summarized gently ('some Jewish readers ... others have noted ...'); a Jewish reviewer as well as a Catholic Keeper should check this line for fairness.
The grafted olive tree alludes to Romans 11:17–18 (paraphrased); confirm.
Practice invites prayer 'in your own simple words or in silence' and offers no new prayer text.
